observations: body L1-L14: the figure stands on the left of these lines and is redrawn from the print: the horizon ABCD about the zenith E (radius 58.9 pt) with the diameters AC and BD, which cross within 0.3 pt of its centre; the half DLB of the ecliptic, an arc of a circle of radius 75.6 pt through B and D; the arc FHP (radius 75.3 pt) from the line GE at F to AC at P; the line from G through E (0.3 pt from the crossing of AC and BD) to K and M; the small circle of the astrolabe (radius 25.9 pt), through whose centre the line KM and the diameter TS pass at right angles. The letters are bold italic.
body L7-L8: the dash before «Schia-» measures 10.4 pt; a heavy bracket closes Schiaparelli's addition begun on p. 271, L36.

body L9, L15-L16, L18, L27-L33, L36: «Al–Battānī» (L9), «ad–dīn» (L15), «aṭ–Ṭūsī» (L16), «Pseudo–Plutarchi» (L18), «318–» (L28), «–19» (L29), «Shù–King» (L31), «2255–2205» (L32), «gemmis–ornatum» (L33) and «1167–1230» (L36) have long dashes (5.3 to 6.0 pt), as have «1890–93» (L28, 4.3 pt) and «15–23» (L30, 6.4 pt); the dash before «Cfr.» (L27) measures 10.4 pt. The year 657 of the Hijra (L16) began on 28 December 1258 by the astronomical epoch of the tables (29 December by the civil), so that it falls almost wholly in 1259.

body L21, L26, L31, L36: «αὐλός» (L21) has the smooth breathing and the acute; «Gamĕlī’ēl» (L26) has a breve over the first e and the apostrophe before «ēl»; «Shù» (L31) has a grave accent; «Ts‘ai C‘in» (L36) has the turned comma of the aspirate twice.

body L19-L23, L31-L38: the addenda (Part I, p. LXXV) add on this page: in the same book V, 1, a little before the passage quoted, Aristotle says «Qui manu sibi obumbrat, aut per fistulam aspicit, differentias colorum nec magis nec minus distinguit, sed longinquius cernit. Item qui interdum e foveis ac puteis astra conspiciunt»; the instrument of the Chinese is perhaps to be compared with the armillary sphere and celestial globe of Gerbert, whose poles a tube pierced that was directed to the constellation of the Little Bear, described by Günther, l. c., p. 16–17; and Nallino does not know whether Abū ’l-‘Alā’ al-Ma‘arrī, the famous poet who died in 449 H. (begun 9 March 1057, by the astronomical epoch of the tables), meant tubes by the word mir’āh in two places quoted by von Kremer, Culturgeschichte des Orients unter den Chalifen, Wien 1875–77, t. II, p. 448.

body L9-L17: Nallino's addenda et emendanda in Part II (pp. XVII-XVIII; AB01-PDF0434-body-L026 to AB01-PDF0435-body-L003), on Part I, p. LXXV and this page, settle the word mir’āh of Abū ’l-‘Alā’ al-Ma‘arrī, of which the addenda of Part I asked whether it meant tubes. The second place quoted by von Kremer is Luzūm, p. 154, line 17 of the Bombay edition (t. I, p. 390 of the Cairo edition), where the astronomer's mir’āh, small as it is, shows him all the tilled land and all the desert; a third place, in his second letter (ed. D. S. Margoliouth, Oxford 1898, p. 18 of the text; Rasā’il, Beirut 1894, pp. 48-49), says of a lexicon that it holds in pure Arabic the place that the astronomer's mir’āh holds in astronomy, whose body is small and compact and yet holds the Sun, the Moon and the stars. It is beyond doubt the astrolabe, as also Ḥāǵǵī Khalīfah's bibliographical lexicon shows: aṣṭurlāb is a Greek word, meaning the balance of the Sun or, as others say, the mir’āh and miqyās of the star, also called in Greek aṣṭurlāfūn, aṣṭur (ἀστήρ) meaning star and lāfūn (λαβών) mir’āh. Compare also the seven verses rhyming in -ūḥ in which the poet Kushāǵim (d. 350 H., begun 19 February 961) describes the astrolabe.

body L27: Nallino's addenda et emendanda in Part II (p. XVIII; AB01-PDF0435-body-L004 to L010) report Suter (Bibl. Math., 3. F., 5. Bd., 1904, p. 81): the diary of Walafrid Strabo, on whose authority modern writers speak of the use of tubes in the European Middle Ages, was forged by P. Marty; yet the notice has some ground, for codex 18 of the Stiftsbibliothek of St. Gall (10th century), p. 43, has a picture of a monk standing on a stool and looking at the sky through a long tube (reproduced in a woodcut in the Mitteilungen der antiquarischen Gesellschaft zu Zürich 19, 1877).
